bank.title: EPTPREP Question Bank
bank.description: Every built-in question, for practice sets you build yourself: choose topics, number of questions and time.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: The **beautiful** garden attracted many visitors.
questions.explanation: "Beautiful" describes the noun "garden", so it is an adjective.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: The students **quickly** finished the test.
questions.explanation: "Quickly" tells us how the students finished, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: She waited **for** the bus.
questions.explanation: "For" links the verb "waited" to the noun phrase "the bus", which is what a preposition does.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: **Honesty** is the best policy.
questions.explanation: "Honesty" names a quality and is the subject of the sentence, so it is an (abstract) noun.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: He is tired **but** happy.
questions.explanation: "But" joins two adjectives of equal rank ("tired" and "happy") and shows contrast, so it is a coordinating conjunction.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly names the word class of the bold word.
questions.prompt: **Wow!** That was a great performance.
questions.explanation: "Wow!" stands on its own to express surprise or admiration, which makes it an interjection.
questions.tip: Ask what job the word does in this sentence: naming (noun), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb), linking (conjunction), showing relation (preposition) or expressing emotion (interjection).

questions.instruction: Choose the correct form of the word to fill the blank.
questions.prompt: The company's ____ increased after the new policy was introduced.
questions.explanation: The possessive "company's" must be followed by a noun, and the noun meaning "rate of output" is "productivity". "Productive" is an adjective and "productively" an adverb.
questions.tip: After a possessive ("the company's") or an article, the gap needs a noun. Look for noun endings such as -ity, -ness, -tion and -ment.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is most appropriate to the field or situation indicated.
questions.prompt: Which of the following words is most associated with the language of the law court?
questions.explanation: A plaintiff is the person who brings a case against another in a court of law. "Patient" belongs to medicine, "tenor" to music and "goalkeeper" to football.
questions.tip: Register questions test the vocabulary that belongs to a profession or setting. Picture the setting (a courtroom, a bank, a hospital, a football match) and pick the word you would actually hear there.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is most appropriate to the field or situation indicated.
questions.prompt: Which of the following words is most associated with banking?
questions.explanation: An overdraft is money withdrawn beyond the balance in a bank account, an arrangement made with a bank. The others belong to the church, the law court and football.
questions.tip: Register questions test the vocabulary that belongs to a profession or setting. Picture the setting (a courtroom, a bank, a hospital, a football match) and pick the word you would actually hear there.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is most appropriate to the field or situation indicated.
questions.prompt: Which of the following words belongs to the register of medicine?
questions.explanation: A prognosis is a doctor's forecast of how an illness will develop. "Cross-examination" and "litigation" are legal terms; "mortgage" belongs to banking and property.
questions.tip: Register questions test the vocabulary that belongs to a profession or setting. Picture the setting (a courtroom, a bank, a hospital, a football match) and pick the word you would actually hear there.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is most appropriate to the field or situation indicated.
questions.prompt: Which of the following sentences is most appropriate in a formal letter of application?
choices: I'm gonna apply for the job.
I wish to apply for the position advertised in your newspaper.
questions.explanation: A formal letter needs polite, complete, impersonal language. The other options are casual ("Hey", "gonna") or blunt commands.
questions.tip: Register questions test the vocabulary that belongs to a profession or setting. Picture the setting (a courtroom, a bank, a hospital, a football match) and pick the word you would actually hear there.

questions.tip: Register questions test the vocabulary that belongs to a profession or setting. Picture the setting (a courtroom, a bank, a hospital, a football match) and pick the word you would actually hear there.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: The principal, together with the teachers, ____ attending the conference.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the principal" (singular); "together with the teachers" is an added phrase that does not make it plural, so the verb is "is".
questions.tip: Find the true subject first. Phrases such as "together with", "as well as" and "along with" add information but do not change the number of the subject.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: Neither the lecturer nor the students ____ aware of the change in the timetable.
questions.explanation: With "neither ... nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "The students" is plural and the sentence is in the past, so "were" is correct.
questions.tip: With "neither ... nor" and "either ... or", the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the rule of proximity).

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: Each of the candidates ____ a separate answer booklet.
questions.explanation: "Each" is singular; "of the candidates" only tells us which group. A singular subject takes "has".
questions.tip: "Each", "every", "either" and "neither" are singular, even when followed by "of" and a plural noun.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: The police ____ investigating the robbery at the bank.
questions.explanation: "Police" is always treated as plural in Standard English, so it takes "are".
questions.tip: Some collective nouns are always plural in form and meaning, e.g. police, people, cattle, clergy.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: A number of applicants ____ submitted their forms late.
questions.explanation: "A number of applicants" means "many applicants", a plural idea, so the verb is "have".
questions.tip: "A number of" means "many" and takes a plural verb; "the number of" refers to one figure and takes a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: The number of unemployed graduates ____ increasing every year.
questions.explanation: "The number" is a single figure and is the head of the subject, so the verb is singular: "is".
questions.tip: "A number of" means "many" and takes a plural verb; "the number of" refers to one figure and takes a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: Ten thousand naira ____ too much to pay for the textbook.
questions.explanation: "Ten thousand naira" is one sum of money considered as a whole, so it takes the singular "is".
questions.tip: Amounts of money, time, distance and weight are treated as a single quantity and take a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Fill in the blank space in each of the following sentences with the most suitable word from the options.
questions.prompt: If I ____ you, I would apply for the postgraduate programme.
questions.explanation: The speaker is not the listener, so the condition is contrary to fact. Standard English uses the subjunctive "were" here, even with "I".
questions.tip: In conditions that are imaginary or contrary to fact ("If I were you..."), use "were" for every subject (the subjunctive).

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: She is intelligent, hardworking and honest.
She is intelligent, hardworking and has honesty.
She is intelligent, works hard and honest.
She is intelligent, hardworking and being honest.
questions.explanation: All three items are adjectives after "is": intelligent, hardworking, honest. The other options switch to a verb phrase or a noun.
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all adjectives, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: Tunde enjoys reading novels, to write poems and watching films.
Tunde enjoys reading novels, writing poems and watching films.
Tunde enjoys to read novels, writing poems and watching films.
Tunde enjoys reading novels, writing poems and to watch films.
questions.explanation: "Enjoy" is followed by -ing forms, and the series stays parallel: reading, writing, watching.
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all adjectives, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: The manager promised to increase salaries, to reduce working hours and improving working conditions.
The manager promised increasing salaries, to reduce working hours and improve conditions.
The manager promised to increase salaries, reduce working hours and improve working conditions.
The manager promised to increase salaries, reduce working hours and to improving conditions.
questions.explanation: One "to" governs three base verbs: (to) increase, reduce, improve. The other options mix infinitives with -ing forms.
questions.tip: When one "to" introduces a series, either use it once before the first item or repeat it before every item, and keep every verb in its base form.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: The new laboratory is spacious, well-equipped and it has good ventilation.
The new laboratory is spacious, equipped well and with ventilation.
The new laboratory is spacious, well-equipped and ventilation is good.
The new laboratory is spacious, well-equipped and well-ventilated.
questions.explanation: Three adjectives describe the laboratory: spacious, well-equipped, well-ventilated. The others end with a clause or phrase instead of an adjective.
questions.tip: When one "to" introduces a series, either use it once before the first item or repeat it before every item, and keep every verb in its base form.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: Ade's duties include marking scripts, setting questions and to supervise projects.
Ade's duties include marking scripts, setting questions and supervising projects.
Ade's duties include to mark scripts, setting questions and supervising projects.
Ade's duties include marking scripts, to set questions and supervising projects.
questions.explanation: Each duty is an -ing phrase: marking scripts, setting questions, supervising projects.
questions.tip: Items in a series must share the same grammatical form: all adjectives, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: The lecture was long, boring and tiring.
The lecture was long, boring and it was tiring.
The lecture was long, bored and tiring.
The lecture was long, boring and tire.
questions.explanation: Three adjectives describe the lecture. "Bored" describes a person's feeling, not the lecture, and "tire" is a verb.
questions.tip: Items in a series must share the same grammatical form: all adjectives, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
choices: She would rather walk to school than to take a taxi.
She would rather walk to school than taking a taxi.
She would rather walk to school than take a taxi.
She would rather walking to school than take a taxi.
questions.explanation: "Would rather" is followed by the bare infinitive on both sides of "than": walk ... take.
questions.tip: In comparisons with "would rather ... than", both sides take the base form of the verb, without "to" or -ing.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the expression that represents the most acceptable parallel structure.
questions.prompt: The speaker was neither rude ____.
questions.explanation: "Neither" pairs with "nor", and "arrogant" is an adjective like "rude", keeping the structure parallel.
questions.tip: "Neither" is paired with "nor", and the word after "nor" must match the word after "neither".

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: The new lecturer promised to **revert back** to the students on Monday.
questions.explanation: "Revert back" repeats itself, and "revert" in this sense is not standard British usage. A British speaker would say "get back to" the students.
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: I could not **cope up with** the workload.
questions.explanation: The standard phrasal verb is "cope with". "Up" is an unnecessary addition.
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: There was a heavy **go-slow** on the expressway this morning.
questions.explanation: In British English a "go-slow" is a form of industrial action; congestion on a road is a "traffic jam".
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: My mother bought a **fairly used** car for me.
questions.explanation: "Fairly used" is Nigerian usage. The standard term for goods that have had a previous owner is "second-hand".
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: My friends came to **send me off** at the airport.
questions.explanation: To accompany someone to their point of departure is to "see them off". "Send off" means to dismiss or dispatch.
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: Please **put off** the lights before you leave.
questions.explanation: Lights and electrical appliances are "switched off" (or "turned off") in standard usage.
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: The lecturer **took permission** to leave early.
questions.explanation: Permission is asked for, sought or obtained, not "taken".
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, select the one that best represents the Standard British English version of each bold word or expression.
questions.prompt: She **passed out** from the university in 2019.
questions.explanation: In British English "pass out" usually means "faint". Completing a university degree is to "graduate".
questions.tip: Many Nigerian expressions add unnecessary words ("revert back", "cope up with"). Remove the extra word, or use the idiom a British speaker would use.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: When Professor Adeyemi entered the hall, the students stood up to greet **him**.
questions.explanation: "Him" is singular and masculine, and the students greeted the person who entered, Professor Adeyemi.
questions.tip: A pronoun usually refers back to the nearest noun that matches it in number and gender and makes sense in context. Replace the pronoun with each option and see which reads correctly.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: Ngozi and Chika are sisters. **The former** is a lawyer, while the latter is a doctor.
questions.explanation: "The former" refers to the first of the two people named, Ngozi.
questions.tip: "The former" points to the first of two things just mentioned; "the latter" points to the second.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: The lecturer returned the scripts after he had marked **them**.
questions.explanation: "Them" is plural and is the thing that was marked, which is the scripts.
questions.tip: A pronoun usually refers back to the nearest noun that matches it in number and makes sense in context.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: Many students applied for the scholarship, but **few** were successful.
choices: Few of the students who applied
questions.explanation: "Few" is short for "few of the students who applied"; the noun is understood from the first clause.
questions.tip: Words such as "few", "many", "some" and "most" can stand for a noun already mentioned (substitution or ellipsis). Work out the full phrase they replace.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: Biola loves jollof rice and cooks **it** every Sunday.
questions.explanation: What Biola cooks is the jollof rice, so "it" refers to "jollof rice".
questions.tip: A pronoun usually refers back to the nearest noun that matches it in number and makes sense in context.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: Seun: Did you read the two novels? Kemi: I read the first but not the **second**.
questions.explanation: "The second" omits the noun "novel", which is understood from Seun's question.
questions.tip: Words such as "the first" and "the second" stand for a noun already mentioned (ellipsis). Supply the missing noun.

questions.instruction: From the options a-d, identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) connect with in each of the sentences or exchanges below.
questions.prompt: Dr. Bello and Dr. Musa teach in the department. **The latter** also supervises postgraduate students.
questions.explanation: "The latter" refers to the second of the two people named, Dr. Musa.
questions.tip: "The former" points to the first of two things just mentioned; "the latter" points to the second.

questions.instruction: Read the passage carefully and answer the question.
questions.passage: Many universities in Nigeria are struggling with a growing problem: students who submit work that is not their own. Lecturers report that, with the arrival of the internet, copying from websites has become so easy that some students no longer see it as wrongdoing. Yet plagiarism, the presentation of another person's ideas or words as one's own, remains a serious academic offence. It damages the reputation of the student, the supervisor and the institution alike. Some institutions now use software that compares submitted work with millions of online sources within minutes. However, experts argue that technology alone cannot solve the problem. They insist that students must be taught to value honest scholarship, to cite their sources properly and to develop the confidence to express their own views. Only then, they say, will degrees earned in Nigerian universities command the respect they deserve.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, why has copying become easier?
choices: The internet has made material readily available.
questions.explanation: The passage says that "with the arrival of the internet, copying from websites has become so easy". The other options are not stated.
questions.tip: Answer from what the passage says, not from your own opinion. Find the sentence that deals with the question and match its meaning, not just its words.

questions.instruction: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: "Millennium" has a double "l" and a double "n": mi-ll-e-nn-ium. It comes from Latin mille (thousand) and annus (year).
questions.tip: Learn the tricky parts of commonly misspelt words: doubled letters (millennium, necessary), "ie/ei" (receive) and silent letters (rhythm, conscience).

questions.instruction: Select the correct sentence in terms of capitalisation.
choices: The Nigerian Army will hold its parade at the University of Ibadan on friday.
The nigerian army will hold its parade at the University of Ibadan on Friday.
The Nigerian Army will hold its parade at the University of Ibadan on Friday.
The Nigerian army will hold its parade at the university of Ibadan on Friday.
questions.explanation: "The Nigerian Army" and "the University of Ibadan" are names of specific institutions, and days of the week always take capitals, so "Friday" is capitalised.
questions.tip: Capitalise proper nouns (specific names of people, institutions, places, days and months) but not general compass directions or common nouns.

questions.instruction: Select the correct sentence in terms of capitalisation.
choices: We travelled north to Kano and then west to the Atlantic Ocean.
We travelled North to Kano and then West to the atlantic ocean.
We travelled north to kano and then west to the Atlantic ocean.
we travelled north to Kano and then west to the Atlantic Ocean.
questions.explanation: "North" and "west" are directions here, so they are lower case. "Kano" and "the Atlantic Ocean" are proper names, and the sentence must begin with a capital.
questions.tip: Capitalise proper nouns (specific names of people, institutions, places, days and months) but not general compass directions or common nouns.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: The students are ready, ____?
questions.explanation: The statement is positive with the auxiliary "are" and a plural subject, so the tag is negative: "aren't they?"
questions.tip: A question tag repeats the auxiliary verb of the statement with the opposite polarity (positive statement, negative tag) and a pronoun for the subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: She can't swim, ____?
questions.explanation: The statement is negative ("can't"), so the tag is positive and repeats the same auxiliary: "can she?"
questions.tip: A question tag repeats the auxiliary verb of the statement with the opposite polarity (positive statement, negative tag) and a pronoun for the subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: Let's go home, ____?
questions.explanation: Suggestions beginning with "Let's" take the tag "shall we?"
questions.tip: Special tags: "Let's ..." takes "shall we?", and imperatives usually take "will you?" (or "won't you?" for invitations).

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: I am invited, ____?
questions.explanation: The positive statement "I am" takes the negative tag "aren't I?" in Standard English.
questions.tip: After "I am", the negative tag is "aren't I?" ("amn't I" is not standard).

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: Nobody called, ____?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive, and indefinite pronouns for people take "they": "did they?"
questions.tip: Negative words such as nobody, nothing, never and hardly make the statement negative, so the tag is positive. "Nobody/everybody" take "they" in the tag.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag to complete each sentence.
questions.prompt: Open the door, ____?
questions.explanation: An imperative (a command) takes the tag "will you?"
questions.tip: Special tags: "Let's ..." takes "shall we?", and imperatives usually take "will you?" (or "won't you?" for invitations).

questions.instruction: Choose the word that best fills each numbered blank in the passage below.
questions.passage:
Library Regulations

Dear students, the University Library Board has recently (61) a new set of rules to (62) the use of library facilities. All students are expected to (63) by these rules at all times. Books borrowed from the lending section must be (64) within fourteen days, and any student who fails to do so will be required to (65) a fine of fifty naira per day. Those who wish to extend the loan period must (66) a formal application to the Librarian. All readers must also (67) strict silence in all reading areas, and anyone who (68) the rules may lose borrowing privileges.
questions.prompt: Choose the best option for blank (61) in the passage.
questions.explanation: Rules, plans and documents are "drawn up" (prepared formally in writing). "Made up" suggests invention.
questions.tip: Collocation questions test which words naturally go together in formal English. Read the whole sentence: the right word fits both the meaning and the words around it (e.g. "abide by", "pay a fine", "observe silence").

questions.instruction: Choose the word that best fills each numbered blank in the passage below.
questions.passage:
Library Regulations

Dear students, the University Library Board has recently (61) a new set of rules to (62) the use of library facilities. All students are expected to (63) by these rules at all times. Books borrowed from the lending section must be (64) within fourteen days, and any student who fails to do so will be required to (65) a fine of fifty naira per day. Those who wish to extend the loan period must (66) a formal application to the Librarian. All readers must also (67) strict silence in all reading areas, and anyone who (68) the rules may lose borrowing privileges.
questions.prompt: Choose the best option for blank (62) in the passage.
questions.explanation: Rules "govern" the use of facilities, meaning they control and regulate it.
questions.tip: Collocation questions test which words naturally go together in formal English. Read the whole sentence: the right word fits both the meaning and the words around it (e.g. "abide by", "pay a fine", "observe silence").

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: He is allergic ____ groundnuts.
questions.explanation: The adjective "allergic" is followed by "to".
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: She is married ____ a medical doctor.
questions.explanation: In Standard English one is married "to" someone.
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: Hardly had the lecture begun ____ the power failed.
questions.explanation: "Hardly" is paired with "when". "Than" goes with "no sooner".
questions.tip: "Hardly/Scarcely ... when" and "No sooner ... than" are fixed pairs; don't mix them.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: Had I known the answer, I ____ you.
questions.explanation: This is a third conditional about the past ("If I had known"), so the result clause is "would have told".
questions.tip: "Had I known" is an inverted third conditional (= "If I had known"), so the main clause takes "would have" + past participle.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: The company decided to ____ the old machines.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb meaning "get rid of" is "dispose of". "Dispose off" is a common error.
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: The new law will come ____ effect next month.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "come into effect", meaning to start to apply.
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: He insisted ____ paying the bill himself.
questions.explanation: "Insist" takes the preposition "on" (insist on doing something).
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.
questions.prompt: She is accustomed ____ waking up early.
questions.explanation: "Accustomed to" is followed by a noun or an -ing form: accustomed to waking up early.
questions.tip: Many adjectives and verbs are followed by a fixed preposition (allergic to, married to, insist on, dispose of). Learn them as pairs.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the item that could be most appropriately used in a letter to your uncle during your visit to his fish farm.
choices: Uncle, more than one fish pond have been flooded by the rain.
Uncle, more than one fish pond has been flooded by the rain.
Uncle, more than one fish pond are been flooded by the rain.
Uncle, more than one fish pond is been flooded by the rain.
questions.explanation: "More than one" is followed by a singular noun and verb ("more than one pond has"). "Is been" and "are been" are not grammatical.
questions.tip: In letter-context questions, the right option is both grammatically correct and suited to the reader. Check concord, tense, spelling (advice/advise) and comparison forms first.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the item that could be most appropriately used in a letter to your uncle during your visit to his fish farm.
choices: The manager, together with the workers, was here yesterday.
The manager, together with the workers, were here yesterday.
The manager, together with the workers, are here yesterday.
The manager, together with the workers, is here yesterday.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the manager" (singular), and "yesterday" requires the past tense, so "was" is correct.
questions.tip: In letter-context questions, the right option is both grammatically correct and suited to the reader. Check concord, tense, spelling (advice/advise) and comparison forms first.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the item that could be most appropriately used in a letter to your uncle during your visit to his fish farm.
choices: I forget my notebook at the hatchery.
I forgotten my notebook at the hatchery.
I have leave my notebook at the hatchery.
I left my notebook at the hatchery.
questions.explanation: When a place is mentioned, use "leave" (past "left"): you leave something somewhere. "Forget" does not normally take a place.
questions.tip: In letter-context questions, the right option is both grammatically correct and suited to the reader. Check concord, tense, spelling (advice/advise) and comparison forms first.

Uncle, I will advise you on the feed to buy.
Uncle, I will advise you to the feed to buy.
Uncle, I will advice you to the feed to buy.
questions.explanation: "Advise" (with s) is the verb and "advice" the noun. We advise someone "on" a matter.
questions.tip: In letter-context questions, the right option is both grammatically correct and suited to the reader. Check concord, tense, spelling (advice/advise) and comparison forms first.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options a-d the item that could be most appropriately used in a letter to your uncle during your visit to his fish farm.
choices: Your farm is more productive than any other farms in the area.
Your farm is more productive than any farm in the area.
Your farm is most productive than any other farm in the area.
Your farm is more productive than any other farm in the area.
questions.explanation: A comparative with "than any other" takes a singular noun ("any other farm"). "Other" is needed because the farm cannot be compared with itself.
questions.tip: In letter-context questions, the right option is both grammatically correct and suited to the reader. Check concord, tense, spelling (advice/advise) and comparison forms first.

questions.instruction: Change the active sentence to the passive structure.
questions.prompt: The workers feed the fish twice daily.
choices: The fish are fed by the workers twice daily.
The fish is fed by the workers twice daily.
The fish were fed by the workers twice daily.
The fish was being fed by the workers twice daily.
questions.explanation: The active verb is present simple, so the passive uses "are" + "fed". "Fish" here refers to many fish, so the verb is plural.
questions.tip: To make a passive, keep the tense of the active verb in the form of "be" and add the past participle; the old object becomes the subject, and the verb agrees with it.

questions.instruction: Change the active sentence to the passive structure.
questions.prompt: My uncle has built a new pond.
choices: A new pond is built by my uncle.
A new pond was built by my uncle.
A new pond has been built by my uncle.
A new pond have been built by my uncle.
questions.explanation: The active verb is present perfect ("has built"), so the passive is "has been built". The subject "a new pond" is singular.
questions.tip: To make a passive, keep the tense of the active verb in the form of "be" and add the past participle; the old object becomes the subject, and the verb agrees with it.

questions.instruction: Change the active sentence to the passive structure.
questions.prompt: They will harvest the fish next week.
choices: The fish are harvested by them next week.
The fish will harvested by them next week.
The fish would be harvest by them next week.
The fish will be harvested by them next week.
questions.explanation: A future active ("will harvest") becomes "will be harvested" in the passive.
questions.tip: To make a passive, keep the tense of the active verb in the form of "be" and add the past participle; the old object becomes the subject, and the verb agrees with it.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best answers each question on the relationships between word meanings.
questions.prompt: "Furniture" is a ____ term for table, chair and bed.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is the general term that includes table, chair and bed; such a general term is a superordinate (the specific words are its hyponyms).
questions.tip: Know the terms: synonymy (same meaning), antonymy (opposite), hyponymy (kind of, e.g. rose/flower), meronymy (part of, e.g. wheel/car), homonymy (same form, unrelated meanings), polysemy (one word, related meanings).

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: The lady likes singing and cooking.
The lady likes singing and to cook.
The lady likes to always sing and cooking.
The lady likes singing and to be cooking.
questions.explanation: "Singing" and "cooking" are both -ing forms (gerunds) after "likes". The other options mix gerunds with infinitives.
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.
questions.source: UI Postgraduate School: Test of English for Higher Degree Admissions, Sample Questions (2013)

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: Dr Ogunmola admires people with character and who seem to have integrity.
Dr Ogunmola admires people who have character as well as people with integrity.
Dr Ogunmola admires people who have character and integrity.
Dr Ogunmola admires people with character and who have integrity.
questions.explanation: One relative clause governs two parallel nouns: "who have character and integrity". The others mix a prepositional phrase ("with character") with a clause.
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.
questions.source: UI Postgraduate School: Test of English for Higher Degree Admissions, Sample Questions (2013)

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: I like to listen, to speak, to read and to do some writing.
I like listening, speaking, reading and writing.
I like listening, speaking, to read, and do writing.
I like listening, speaking, reading, writing.
questions.explanation: All four items are -ing forms joined by "and" before the last item. Option (d) leaves out the conjunction, and (a) breaks the pattern with "to do some writing".
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.
questions.source: UI Postgraduate School: Test of English for Higher Degree Admissions, Sample Questions (2013)

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: He was bruised for our iniquities and crushed for our transgressions.
He showed forgiveness for our iniquities, he was crushed for our transgressions.
He was bruised for our iniquities, and they were always crushing him for all our transgressions.
He was bruised for our iniquities, and was also to be crushed for our transgressions.
questions.explanation: Two passive participles with the same pattern: "bruised for our iniquities" and "crushed for our transgressions".
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.

The writing of a good student should be precise and show originality.

questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.

questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.

questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.
questions.source: UI Postgraduate School: Test of English for Higher Degree Admissions, Sample Questions (2013)

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: The prophet predicted that he would become governor; that he would meet a beautiful stranger and that his first son would become president.
The prophet predicted that he would become governor; a beautiful stranger will meet him and that his first son would become president.
The prophet predicted that he would become governor; he would meet a beautiful stranger; his first son would become president.
The prophet predicted that he would become governor; a beautiful stranger, will meet him; his son, to become a future president.
questions.explanation: Each prediction is a "that" clause with "would": that he would become ..., that he would meet ..., that his first son would become ....
questions.tip: Items joined by "and", "or", "but" or listed in a series must share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing forms, all "to" infinitives, all clauses, and so on.

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.
choices: I was writing the letter when she lays the table for breakfast.
I was writing the letter when she laid the table for breakfast.
I was writing the letter while she lay the table for breakfast.
I was writing the letter while she was laying the table for breakfast.
questions.explanation: Two actions in progress at the same time are both in the past continuous: "was writing ... was laying". Note also "lay" (put down) has the -ing form "laying".
questions.tip: When two actions happen at the same time in the past, keep both verbs in the same tense and aspect (e.g. past continuous with past continuous).
questions.source: UI Postgraduate School: Test of English for Higher Degree Admissions, Sample Questions (2013)

questions.instruction: Choose from the options written against letters a-d the expression that represents the most standard/acceptable structure.

questions.instruction: Read the passage and answer the question.
questions.passage:
Every discernible observer could foresee the crisis which engulfed the Edo House last week. Only a few days before, reports were rife about the AC reaching out to some PDP legislators to cross-carpet, the intention being to gain a majority and then assume the Speakership with the least constraint. Zakawanu Garuba, the then Speaker, retorted with a fiat, threatening to declare vacant the seat of any defector. This in spite of the constitutional support for such action, as evidenced, for example, by the crisis that has torn the PDP apart in Edo State. The party has two factional chairmen in the state, even though one is more vociferous.

The desperate attempt by Garuba to cling to the Speaker's chair is condemnable. He was not being recalled from the legislature; and so, he still has his seat as a floor member. As Speaker, he was only first among equals. The Speakership is not his birthright. With the defection of one PDP lawmaker to the AC, the legislature reconvened hours after the bloodbath and elected a protem Speaker, while impeaching and suspending Garuba and a few others. They are to be probed.

(Adapted from The Guardian, 4 March 2011)
questions.prompt: Why did the AC woo PDP members?
questions.explanation: The passage says the intention was "to gain a majority and then assume the Speakership with the least constraint", i.e. without stress.

questions.instruction: Read the passage and answer the question.
questions.passage:
Nigeria has a troubled power sector which is however undergoing reforms that, hopefully, should usher in an era of private sector dominance in terms of ownership and management of generation and distribution. In this transitory phase, it is crucial to lay a foundation for local sourcing of vital inputs and make it the norm for the industry. That is the only way to prevent a replication of the trend in the oil and gas sub-sector, where capital flight is as much as $16 billion per annum, as revealed by the Petroleum Technology Development Fund.

The PHCN could legitimately insist on quality and standards in its procurement of equipment and materials, but what is playing out is an institutional orientation, evinced in several pursuits of the PHCN, that is contemptuous of Nigeria's aspiration for local content development. In 1998, the defunct National Electric Power Authority defied a directive by the then Minister of Power and Steel, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, to source its castable components from Nigerian foundries, some of which are of high standards. Actuated by a realisation of idle capacity in the foundries and the need to conserve foreign exchange, the Minister applied appropriate pressure on the management of NEPA but found his efforts frustrated. The acute shortage or inefficiency in the metering programme originated from the fact that the only local manufacturer then, the Federal Government-owned Electricity Meter Company in Zaria, Kaduna State, established in 1976 but sold to Dantata Investments Limited in December 2002, is not performing.

(Adapted from The Punch, 25 May 2011)

choices: Non-performance of the Federal Government-owned Electricity Meter Company
questions.explanation: The shortage "originated from the fact that the only local manufacturer ... the Federal Government-owned Electricity Meter Company ... is not performing".

questions.prompt: University students ____ behave well.

questions.instruction: Pick out the odd/wrong expression in each of the following.
choices: I suppose you know the way
I am supposed you know the way
I suppose he knows the way
They suppose he knows the way
questions.explanation: "I am supposed you know" is ungrammatical: "suppose" meaning "think" is active ("I suppose ..."), while "be supposed" needs "to" + verb.
questions.tip: A dangling participle is one whose implied subject is not the subject of the main clause. The person who did the -ing action must be the subject that follows the comma.
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.instruction: Pick out the odd/wrong expression in each of the following.

questions.instruction: Pick out the odd/wrong expression in each of the following.

questions.explanation: "If I go" (present) needs "will/can" in the main clause; "would" belongs with "if I went".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the gap.

questions.explanation: A positive statement with "are" takes the negative tag "aren't you?" ("are'nt" is misspelt).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the gap.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the gap.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the gap.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the gap.

questions.instruction: Identify the grammatical name or function of the bold expression.

questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).

questions.prompt: I'm proud **of you**. The bold expression functions as
questions.explanation: "Of you" completes the meaning of the adjective "proud", so it is an adjectival complement.
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.instruction: Identify the grammatical name or function of the bold expression.
questions.prompt: A noun phrase lacks one of the following:
questions.explanation: A noun phrase is built around a noun and may contain adjectives and adverbs, but it has no verb.
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.instruction: Identify the grammatical name or function of the bold expression.
questions.prompt: Eve gave Adam **an apple**. "An apple" in the sentence functions as
questions.explanation: "An apple" is the thing given (direct object); "Adam" is the receiver (indirect object).
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.instruction: Identify the grammatical name or function of the bold expression.
questions.prompt: I wonder if you know where he lives. This sentence is a(n)
questions.explanation: It reports a question inside a statement ("I wonder if ..."), which is an indirect question. (The PDF's key gives "thoughtful statement".)
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.instruction: Identify the grammatical name or function of the bold expression.
questions.prompt: An example of a gradable adjective is
questions.explanation: Gradable adjectives can be intensified or compared ("very beautiful", "more beautiful"); "dead" and "live" are not normally graded.
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
questions.source: University of Ibadan Post-UTME Practice Questions: Use of English

questions.prompt: A clause differs from a phrase because a clause contains
questions.explanation: A clause has a finite verb (with tense and subject); a phrase does not.
questions.tip: A clause has a finite verb; a phrase does not. Name the unit by its form (clause, phrase) and its function (adverbial of time, appositive, complement).
