questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: So far, three days ____ been spent on this.
questions.explanation: Following UI's sample-paper key, a period of time treated as one unit takes "has".
questions.tip: Periods of time and amounts seen as one unit take a singular verb; "minutes" (of a meeting) is plural; names of diseases ending in -s are singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The new army barracks ____ close to my house.
questions.explanation: "The new army barracks" here is one military base, so the verb is singular.
questions.tip: Periods of time and amounts seen as one unit take a singular verb; "minutes" (of a meeting) is plural; names of diseases ending in -s are singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Snakes and Ladders ____ interesting.
questions.explanation: "Snakes and Ladders" is the name of one game, so it takes the singular "is".
questions.tip: Titles of games, books and films are singular even when they look plural.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Ten litres of petrol ____ enough.
questions.explanation: "Ten litres of petrol" is one quantity, so "is".
questions.tip: Amounts of liquid, money or time viewed as one quantity take a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Omoope and Associates ____ my first choice for this contract.
questions.explanation: "Omoope and Associates" is the name of one firm, so "is".
questions.tip: The name of a firm is singular even when it contains "and".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Dr Eben, Jesse and Emmanuel ____ to play.
questions.explanation: Three people joined by "and" form a plural subject, so "love".
questions.tip: Subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb, unless they name one person or one thing.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: His sister and confidant ____ arrived.
questions.explanation: "His sister and confidant" is one person (his sister, who is also his confidant), so the verb is singular.
questions.tip: Subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb, unless they name one person or one thing.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Yam and egg ____ my favourite meal.
questions.explanation: "Yam and egg" is one dish, so it takes the singular "is".
questions.tip: Subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb, unless they name one person or one thing.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Ben ____ a lot.
questions.explanation: "Ben" is third-person singular, so "talks".
questions.tip: Third-person singular subjects take -s in the present simple; plural subjects do not.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The boys ____ in the choir.
questions.explanation: "The boys" is plural, so the verb has no -s.
questions.tip: Third-person singular subjects take -s in the present simple; plural subjects do not.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The mice ____ dead.
questions.explanation: "Mice" is the plural of "mouse", so "are".
questions.tip: Irregular plurals (mice, feet, teeth, children, people) take plural verbs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: My feet ____ cold.
questions.explanation: "Feet" is plural, so "are".
questions.tip: Irregular plurals (mice, feet, teeth, children, people) take plural verbs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The retired military officer is one of the past leaders who ____ the embodiment of corruption.
questions.explanation: "Who" refers to "the past leaders" (plural), so the verb in the relative clause is "are".
questions.tip: In "one of the ... who ...", the verb after "who" agrees with the plural noun.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Each of the ____ must wait behind.
questions.explanation: After "each of", the noun is plural ("the girls"), although the verb that follows is singular.
questions.tip: "Each of", "either of" and "neither of" are followed by a plural noun and a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Neither Dr Whales nor his friends ____ how to swim.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, "his friends", is plural, so "know".
questions.tip: With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Every cow and goat ____ grass.
questions.explanation: "Every" makes the subject singular: every cow and (every) goat eats grass.
questions.tip: "Every" makes a compound subject singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: All but Admin ____ asleep.
questions.explanation: The subject is "all" (everyone except Admin), which is plural.
questions.tip: "All but X" means "all except X", and the verb agrees with "all" (plural for people).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Either Celxius or Squpho ____ coming for the ceremony.
questions.explanation: Two singular subjects joined by "either ... or" take a singular verb.
questions.tip: With "either ... or", the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Much of the fuel I bought ____ evaporated.
questions.explanation: "Much of the fuel" is an uncountable quantity, so "has".
questions.tip: "Much of" + uncountable noun takes a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: I pray that God ____ you with your struggles.
questions.explanation: After "pray that", formal English uses the subjunctive base form: "God help you".
questions.tip: After "I pray that", "I insist that" and similar, formal English uses the subjunctive (base form, no -s).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Everyone ____ annoying me.
questions.explanation: "Everyone" is singular, so "is".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, everybody, someone, no one, nothing take singular verbs.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: If Akinyele passes the EPT, Admin, Dr Whales, Dosunmu or his friends ____ to thank.
questions.explanation: The nearest subject, "his friends", is plural, so "are".
questions.tip: With "or", the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: A pair of trousers ____ on the bed.
questions.explanation: The head of the subject is "pair" (singular), so "is".
questions.tip: "A pair of" + plural noun takes a singular verb, because the head word is "pair".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The manager together with her workers ____ lazy.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the manager" (singular); "together with her workers" is an added phrase.
questions.tip: Phrases such as "together with" and "as well as" do not change the number of the subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The police, not the criminal, ____ to blame.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with "the police" (always plural); "not the criminal" is an aside.
questions.tip: When a subject is followed by "not ...", the verb agrees with the affirmative subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: One of the elders who ____ generously was honoured.
questions.explanation: "Who" refers to "the elders" (plural), so the verb in the relative clause is "give".
questions.tip: In "one of the ... who ...", the verb after "who" agrees with the plural noun.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The series of killings ____ me scared.
questions.explanation: "The series" (one sequence of killings) is singular, so "makes".
questions.tip: "Series" referring to one set of things is singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Most of the issues ____ internal.
questions.explanation: "Most of the issues" refers to plural issues, so "are".
questions.tip: "Most of" + plural noun takes a plural verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: One of the robbers ____ escaped.
questions.explanation: The subject is "one" (of the robbers), which is singular, so "has".
questions.tip: "Each" and indefinite pronouns are singular; plural numbers ("four of my friends") are plural.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Four of my friends ____ coming.
questions.explanation: "Four of my friends" is plural, so "are".
questions.tip: "Each" and indefinite pronouns are singular; plural numbers ("four of my friends") are plural.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: This means of transport ____ the best.
questions.explanation: "This means" refers to one method of transport, so "is".
questions.tip: "Means" (a method) has the same form in singular and plural; "this means" is singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: All the members of the family ____ excited.
questions.explanation: "All the members" is plural, so "are".
questions.tip: Collective nouns (family, staff, majority) take a plural verb when the members are thought of as individuals.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The staff ____ earned many awards this year.
questions.explanation: "The staff" here refers to the individual employees who earned awards, so British usage takes the plural "have".
questions.tip: Collective nouns (family, staff, majority) take a plural verb when the members are thought of as individuals.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The majority of people ____ interested in sport.
questions.explanation: "The majority of people" refers to many individuals, so the verb is plural.
questions.tip: Collective nouns (family, staff, majority) take a plural verb when the members are thought of as individuals.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Minority parties ____ grown over the past two years.
questions.explanation: "Minority parties" is plural, so "have".
questions.tip: Collective nouns (family, staff, majority) take a plural verb when the members are thought of as individuals.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Members of the navy ____ called sailors.
questions.explanation: "Members" is the plural head of the subject.
questions.tip: Collective nouns (family, staff, majority) take a plural verb when the members are thought of as individuals.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Everybody ____ her.
questions.explanation: "Everybody" is singular, so "likes".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one and -thing are singular, as is "anywhere" used as a subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: No one ____ tomorrow.
questions.explanation: "No one" is singular, so "knows".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one and -thing are singular, as is "anywhere" used as a subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Everything here ____ beautiful.
questions.explanation: "Everything" is singular, so "is".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one and -thing are singular, as is "anywhere" used as a subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Anywhere you take me ____ fine by me.
questions.explanation: The noun clause "anywhere you take me" acts as a single subject, so "is".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one and -thing are singular, as is "anywhere" used as a subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Somebody ____ them the secret.
questions.explanation: "Somebody" is singular, so "tells".
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one and -thing are singular, as is "anywhere" used as a subject.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: More than one member ____ protested against the proposal.
questions.explanation: "More than one member" takes a singular verb.
questions.tip: "More than one" + singular noun takes a singular verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Two-thirds of the area ____ under water.
questions.explanation: "Area" is singular, so "two-thirds of the area is".
questions.tip: Fractions take the number of the noun after "of": "two-thirds of the area" (singular area) is singular.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Medical research shows that measles ____ a person only once in a lifetime.
questions.explanation: "Measles" is the name of a disease and is singular.
questions.tip: Plural subjects take the base form of the verb in the present simple.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Messi has won five Ballon d'Or awards and some see him as the best. This is a **fact**.
choices: He has won five Ballon d'Or awards
He is the best and has won five Ballon d'Or awards
questions.explanation: The study group's key takes "this" as referring to the whole preceding sentence. (Strictly, only the five awards are a fact; "the best" is an opinion.)
questions.tip: Summary nouns ("fact", "issue", "problem") refer back to a whole statement. Pick the option that restates exactly what the earlier sentence claims.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: I just got a new toothbrush, unlike **the former**.
questions.explanation: "The former" here means the earlier (old) toothbrush, contrasted with the new one.
questions.tip: "The former" refers to the first of two things mentioned; "the latter" to the second.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Lightoj can speak Yoruba and French; I can't speak **any**.
questions.explanation: "I can't speak any" refers to the two languages mentioned, meaning "I can't speak either of them".
questions.tip: Negative replies with "any" or "either" pick up the items just mentioned.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Oh! There **you** are, my cute little kitten.
questions.explanation: "You" points forward to the vocative "my cute little kitten"; of the options, (c) gives the full phrase.
questions.tip: A pronoun can point forward (cataphora) to a noun phrase that comes later.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: I gave out a lot of my cutlery; **many more** were returned to me.
choices: A few more than I gave
questions.explanation: "Many more" (than I gave out) means more pieces came back than were given.
questions.tip: Quantity expressions such as "many more" are interpreted against an amount already mentioned.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Betty: Which shirt are you wearing this morning? Dr Whales: I will wear my black **round neck**.
questions.explanation: "Round neck" describes the shirt; the noun "shirt" is understood from the question.
questions.tip: Words like "round neck" can stand for a noun from the question (ellipsis): "my black round neck (shirt)".

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: I could have beaten her, but I decided **not to**.
choices: I would not do such a thing
questions.explanation: "Not to" stands for "not to beat her", so the meaning is that I did not beat her.
questions.tip: In ellipsis, part of a clause is left out because it can be recovered. Rebuild the full clause.

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Tobitools, Blaise, Niel, Honfikky and Modepeayo are active members on the page, just to mention a **few**.
choices: These are some names among the many active members
These are the names of the most active members
questions.explanation: "Just to mention a few" signals that the names listed are only some of the many active members.
questions.tip: "A few" after a list means "some among many".

questions.instruction: Identify the word or expression that the bold word(s) refer to.
questions.prompt: Phemmy is always honest with his scores on the page; **he** doesn't lie.
questions.explanation: "He" refers to Phemmy. The other options add descriptions not in the text.
questions.tip: A pronoun refers back to the noun it matches and makes sense with.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Ben works for ____ European company.
questions.explanation: "European" begins with a "y" sound, so it takes "a".
questions.tip: Use "a" before a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound: "a European" (starts with a "y" sound), "an honest" (silent h).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: ____ honest man is hard to find.
questions.explanation: "Honest" begins with a silent "h" and a vowel sound, so it takes "an".
questions.tip: Use "a" before a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound: "a European" (starts with a "y" sound), "an honest" (silent h).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The dog chased Ojo and ____.
questions.explanation: "Me" is the object of "chased".
questions.tip: After a verb or preposition, use object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Those men helped Bola and ____.
questions.explanation: "Me" is the object of "helped". (The group's key gave "I", which is wrong after a verb.)
questions.tip: After a verb or preposition, use object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: In "10 o'clock", the "o" stands for
questions.explanation: "O'clock" is a contraction of "of the clock".
questions.tip: Some abbreviations hide a word: "o'clock" is short for "of the clock".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: He is insistent ____ doing the job.
questions.explanation: "Insistent on" (like "insist on") is the standard combination.
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Bilikisu has shown enough aversion ____ science.
questions.explanation: The standard combination is "aversion to". (The group's key gave "for".)
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Do you know how good he is ____ Maths?
questions.explanation: We are good "at" a subject or activity.
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: They are worse ____ physics than we thought.
questions.explanation: "Worse at" follows the same pattern as "good at".
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The boy was charged ____ attempted theft.
questions.explanation: One is "charged with" an offence.
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: He was lucky he was not convicted ____ the crime.
questions.explanation: One is "convicted of" a crime. (The group's key gave "for".)
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Their father deals ____ expensive shoes.
questions.explanation: To "deal in" goods is to buy and sell them.
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The teacher decided to translate his lectures ____ the local languages.
questions.explanation: One translates "into" another language.
questions.tip: Many adjectives, nouns and verbs take a fixed preposition. Learn them as pairs: insist on, aversion to, good at, preside over, convicted of, deal in, translate into.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The dog broke ____ leg.
questions.explanation: "Its" is the possessive; "it's" means "it is".
questions.tip: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs) never take an apostrophe.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The bag isn't mine but ____.
questions.explanation: The possessive pronoun "yours" has no apostrophe.
questions.tip: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs) never take an apostrophe.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The man ____ his clothes on the wire.
questions.explanation: Clothes are "hung". "Hanged" is only used for executing a person. (The group's key gave "hanged".)
questions.tip: "Hang" has two past forms: "hung" for objects, "hanged" only for executing a person.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The army ran short of ____.
questions.explanation: "Arms" (weapons) is always plural, and "ammunition" is uncountable.
questions.tip: Some nouns are uncountable in English (furniture, equipment, information, luggage) and some appear only in the plural (arms meaning weapons, amends).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: We left a lot of ____ at the factory.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" and "equipment" are uncountable and have no plural form.
questions.tip: Some nouns are uncountable in English (furniture, equipment, information, luggage) and some appear only in the plural (arms meaning weapons, amends).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: We promise to make ____.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "make amends", with one "m" and a final "s".
questions.tip: Some nouns are uncountable in English (furniture, equipment, information, luggage) and some appear only in the plural (arms meaning weapons, amends).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The helpless ____ our sympathy.
questions.explanation: "The helpless" means helpless people, so the verb is plural: "require".
questions.tip: "The + adjective" (the helpless, the poor, the rich) refers to a group of people and takes a plural verb.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Their father gave us six fifteen-____ jars.
questions.explanation: In a compound adjective ("fifteen-litre jars"), the measurement word stays singular.
questions.tip: A number + measurement used as an adjective before a noun stays singular and is hyphenated: "a fifteen-litre jar".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The president of the ____ union has been rusticated.
questions.explanation: It is the union belonging to the students, so the plural possessive "students' union".
questions.tip: A noun used to describe another noun can be possessive plural: "the students' union" (the union of the students).

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: The politician hardly visits anybody; he trusts ____ of his associates.
questions.explanation: "Hardly visits anybody" suggests he trusts almost none of them: "few" (not many). "Associates" is countable, so not "little".
questions.tip: "Few" (hardly any) is negative; "a few" (some) is positive. "Little/a little" work the same way with uncountable nouns.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: All the four boys ____ detained.
questions.explanation: "The four boys" is plural, so "are being detained".
questions.tip: Progressive passive: "are being" + past participle; after "was", "being" + past participle.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Ballanda was ____ deceived by the magician.
questions.explanation: The past continuous passive is "was being deceived".
questions.tip: Progressive passive: "are being" + past participle; after "was", "being" + past participle.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Tunji has ____ the idea of going overseas.
questions.explanation: "Burst" has the same form in the past participle ("has burst"). (Strictly, one "bursts" a bubble; the item tests the verb form.)
questions.tip: Learn the principal parts of irregular verbs: burst-burst-burst, grind-ground-ground, shake-shook-shaken, freeze-froze-frozen, flee-fled-fled, sew-sewed-sewn.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.
questions.prompt: Have you ____ the pepper at the shop?
questions.explanation: The past participle of "grind" is "ground".
questions.tip: Learn the principal parts of irregular verbs: burst-burst-burst, grind-ground-ground, shake-shook-shaken, freeze-froze-frozen, flee-fled-fled, sew-sewed-sewn.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

questions.instruction: Read the passage and answer the question.
questions.passage:
The permanent conversion of farmland to urban and industrial development is a major concern today. Accurate data on the rate of such losses are not available, but estimates for the area of land absorbed for every increase of 1,000 in the urban population vary from about 10 to 400 hectares. The higher figure includes urban fringe land alienated from agriculture by land speculation and resulting high prices. If an average figure of 80 hectares for every increase of 1,000 in the urban population is used, the projected permanent conversion of land to urban development in Quebec and Ontario is 300,000 hectares and 500,000 hectares respectively. More than half of this land is good agricultural land in climatically favourable areas. Around Montreal, for instance, 8,700 hectares of the best agricultural land in Quebec is being lost to development each year. Equally serious may be the loss of farmland to low-density rural housing, but no firm data are available.

There is a similar trend in Western Canada. About 40,000 hectares of farmland were lost to urban development between 1962 and 1972. In Alberta, over 16,000 hectares of prime land were absorbed in the course of seven years by the cities of Edmonton and Calgary, and there is evidence that smaller towns on the Prairies are consuming farmland at up to twice the rate, per unit population, of the big cities. The areas mentioned may not seem impressive in relation to the total area of farmland in Canada, and it is true that few statistics are available on the rates of loss of farmland. However, the picture is clear enough to provide the basis for rational choices.

It must be remembered that only tiny areas of Canada, less than one per cent, have climates and soils suitable for the production of corn and soft fruits. Most of these valuable parcels of land are in the path of rapid urban and industrial growth. Productive farmland close to the city is basic insurance against future events such as food shortages and high prices that would result from: (a) a dramatic increase in the world's population; (b) a climatic shift such as a decrease of even a degree or two in the mean annual temperature; (c) a series of dry years; or (d) increasingly high transportation costs due to energy shortages.

Because of its "greenbelt" character, farmland is also of immeasurable aesthetic value. City dwellers will often drive for miles to experience an orchard in blossom and enjoy the rural scene. Wildlife ecologists have persuaded us of the value of preserving endangered species like the whooping crane and of the necessity of selecting pipeline routes that will not disturb migrating animals like the caribou. Surely it is not too much to expect that we recognize the necessity of preserving for agriculture the prime farmland close to cities such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
questions.prompt: The main idea of this passage is that in Canada
choices: urban and industrial growth should be slowed down.
losses of farmland constitute an important problem.
accurate statistics on farmland conversion are needed.
prime farmland is scarce in areas of good climate.
questions.explanation: The passage opens by calling farmland conversion "a major concern" and ends by urging that it be stopped; the other options are supporting details.
questions.tip: For main-idea questions, choose the option that covers the whole passage, not just one detail. For detail questions, find the exact sentence before deciding.
questions.source: CanTEST sample test (Sheridan English Proficiency Assessment)

questions.passage: The potato, like other root crops, has an unearned reputation in some countries as an inferior food, or a poor person's staple. While roots are the main ingredient of the diet of half a million people, the potato's nutritive content of protein, fibre, minerals, and vitamins B1, B2 and C hardly makes it inferior. Medical researchers report that potatoes are even better than milk for malnourished children, who often cannot digest milk. Potatoes provide a high-quality protein similar to that in dairy products. Unfortunately, the potato is still out of reach of a poor person's budget in many developing countries such as Indonesia and the Philippines.
questions.prompt: According to this passage, why might potatoes be better than milk for children who are improperly nourished?
choices: Potatoes contain quite a bit of calcium.
Potatoes have more B vitamins than milk.
These children often cannot assimilate milk.
These children often cannot find a supply.
questions.explanation: The passage says malnourished children "often cannot digest milk"; "assimilate" means absorb or digest.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.
questions.source: UN Language Proficiency Examination (English) practice paper

questions.passage: "Anting" is a noun that is entering the language because of ornithologists, or bird watchers. Anting refers to an activity in which birds rub themselves with defence fluids or, sometimes, other bodily fluids of ants. In the past scientists thought anting had no function and that it was a vice like smoking or drinking. However, most ornithologists now think that birds use ant fluids to kill parasites. Among those ants that birds favour are the Azteca ants, which produce formic acid, a repellent so effective that it will drive off army ants. Birds often crash dive into Azteca nests and allow the insects to crawl all over their bodies, or they grasp them in their beaks and rub them through their feathers. The birds get such relief from their treatment that some appear to swoon and even lose their balance.
questions.prompt: "Anting" ____.
choices: is an activity unique to bird watchers
refers to the killing of Azteca ants by parasites
is a relatively new word in the English language
refers to the way ants defend themselves
questions.explanation: The first sentence says "anting" is a noun "that is entering the language", so it is a new word.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.
questions.source: UN Language Proficiency Examination (English) practice paper

questions.passage: Tall children score slightly higher on intelligence tests and perform somewhat better academically than their shorter classmates, perhaps because more is expected of them, researchers for a National Health Examination survey have found. The magnitude of the difference is not large, however, and certainly not worth giving children growth hormones to make them taller, said Dr. Darrell Wilson of Stanford University. He and his colleagues concluded there was a definite link between height and scores on tests of both intelligence and achievement. The association remained even after controlling for other factors, including socioeconomic status, birth order, family size and rate of physical maturity. Dr. Wilson said the difference was small but significant. The researchers based their findings on data from a study involving nearly 14,000 children from six to 17 years old.
questions.prompt: One cause the researchers suggested for the connection between height and test scores was the tall children's ____.
questions.explanation: The researchers suggest tall children do better "perhaps because more is expected of them".
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.

questions.passage: Tall children score slightly higher on intelligence tests and perform somewhat better academically than their shorter classmates, perhaps because more is expected of them, researchers for a National Health Examination survey have found. The magnitude of the difference is not large, however, and certainly not worth giving children growth hormones to make them taller, said Dr. Darrell Wilson of Stanford University. He and his colleagues concluded there was a definite link between height and scores on tests of both intelligence and achievement. The association remained even after controlling for other factors, including socioeconomic status, birth order, family size and rate of physical maturity. Dr. Wilson said the difference was small but significant. The researchers based their findings on data from a study involving nearly 14,000 children from six to 17 years old.
questions.prompt: The researchers found that the difference between the test scores of tall and short children ____.
choices: can be linked to socioeconomic status
is meaningful although it is small
questions.explanation: Dr Wilson said "the difference was small but significant"; the link remained after controlling for socioeconomic status.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.

questions.passage: Worker involvement in the protection of health at work is gaining ground in the European Economic Community (EEC), where most States have overhauled their national laws on job safety during the past decade. Today, worker representatives should be informed and consulted on health and safety matters and they are entitled in one way or another to inspect workplaces and investigate accidents. The watchdog role is assigned to statutory work councils, safety delegates and voluntary bodies. But what rights do EEC workers actually enjoy, and how much real use have they made of them? A study of these questions recently published by the ILO reveals a chequered picture of greatly varying approaches and degrees of success.

worker groups do not have enough power to enforce safety laws
questions.explanation: The study reveals "a chequered picture of greatly varying approaches and degrees of success", i.e. uneven results.

questions.passage: A long time back a reviewer ridiculed William Carlos Williams for saying one reason a poet wrote was to become a better person. I was fresh out of graduate school and I easily sided with the reviewer. But now I see Williams was right. I do not think Williams was advocating writing as therapy, nor the naive idea that after writing a poem one is less depraved. I believe Williams discovered that a lifetime of writing was a slow, accumulative way of accepting one's life as valid. We sweat through poem after poem to realize what dumb animals know by instinct and reveal in their behaviour: my life is all I have got. We are off to know ourselves, even if our method of learning is painfully convoluted.
questions.prompt: The author of this passage has come to realize the value of writing as ____.
choices: a means of coming to terms with your existence
an efficient way of understanding your true feelings
an aid to help you better understand your world
a potential therapy for your instinctive behaviour
questions.explanation: Writing is "a slow, accumulative way of accepting one's life as valid", i.e. coming to terms with one's existence. The writer rejects the idea of therapy and calls the method "convoluted", not efficient.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.

questions.passage: There is a special kind of person who is more likely than most to take the first step to help and to stay with the effort to the end: the altruist. According to Dr. Staub, "There is a pattern of child-rearing that seems to encourage altruism in later years. A warm and nurturing relationship between parent and child is essential, but not enough in itself. The parents who transmit altruism most effectively exert a firm control over their children. Although they are nurturing, they are not permissive. They use a combination of firmness, warmth and reasoning. They point out to children the consequences to others of misbehaviour, and good behaviour. And they actively guide the child to do good, to share, to be helpful."

were not only encouraging but also strict
taught them that misbehaviour deserves punishment
questions.explanation: Effective parents are "nurturing" but "not permissive", combining "firmness, warmth and reasoning".

questions.passage:
To many developing countries, tourism has appeared to be a bonanza, a source of precious foreign exchange, a stimulant to foreign investment in splendid hotels and a creator of employment in service industries. Now there are many second thoughts as the real cost in economic distortion and pollution of the social environment is totalled up.

The distortion arises from land speculation in tourist areas, inflation of land values in principal cities and the unbalanced development that caters to the requirements of pleasure seekers from abroad as much as to the needs of the indigenous people. Roads, water supply and telecommunications are often designed with tourism primarily in mind. One critic estimates that infrastructural expenses of this kind, plus imports of luxury items to create creature comforts for visitors, consume more than two thirds of the foreign exchange derived from tourism.

But such economic costs may well be less than the psycho-social impact. At a recent international conference, the mischief wrought by the tourist industry was frequently referred to as catastrophic, especially in those areas described in travel folders as "unspoilt paradises". The conferees agreed that all too often travel does not heighten understanding between peoples of different cultures but intensifies prejudices on both sides and, among the host people, creates imitation, frustration, loss of traditional authenticity, commercialized hospitality and xenophobia.

This process has of course been observed before now, but it has been vastly accelerated by the speed, convenience and reach of the jet plane and by the economic feasibility of travel for masses of people. In Africa, for example, tourism is the most rapidly developing industry, with annual growth rates of 20 to 40 per cent in some countries. Moreover, the predominance of the packaged tour virtually precludes any real contact with local people and presents the traveller, not as an individual fellow human, but as a member of a closed party.

Though developing countries may be the most vulnerable, no country is immune. This year it is expected that visitors to one small Mediterranean country will outnumber the country's total population. To accommodate them, the most beautiful parts of the country's coast have been converted into tawdry vacationlands which create monumental pollution. So pervasive are the tourists there that the natives often feel like strangers in their own land. Though it may be too late to save this country, is there anything that can be done for areas where the numbers are not yet so great? Better education of both tourists and hosts seems the only hope.
questions.prompt: According to the author of the text, tourism in developing countries ____.
choices: has been an invaluable stimulant to economic development
may not be as economically beneficial as was originally hoped
has had greater economic costs than psycho-social impact
has become a total social and economic disaster for all concerned
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says there are "many second thoughts" as the real costs are totalled up; (d) is too extreme and (c) reverses the text.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.
questions.source: UN Language Proficiency Examination (English) practice paper

questions.passage:
It is just before dawn and the garden cross spider is getting ready for another hot summer's day. It is still dark, and being cold-blooded, he is feeling rather chilly. But he gets up and eats a few key strands of his web, and then sets about spinning a new one to serve for the coming day.

Theories abound as to why garden cross spiders (and most other web-building spiders) should find this seemingly pointless daily ritual necessary, and why they should do it in the cold pre-dawn. Researchers at Oxford University believe they have found at least part of the answer. The spiders are not eating their webs; they are drinking them.

Water is a big problem for spiders. Their lungs must be kept moist, but they lose a lot of liquid during the course of the day. Hunting spiders can wander off for a drink if they are thirsty, but web-builders must stick around, as it were, for their prey. Worse still, their webs are generally built in exposed places: good for catching flies, but bad for getting dried out by the wind. Flies are juicy, and satisfy thirst as well as hunger, but if they are scarce, the spiders have a problem.

The researchers found that the webs catch a lot of moisture, as well as flies. By eating its web, a spider can take up enough water to restore 10 per cent of its daily respiratory loss. Webs are consumed in the humid pre-dawn because this is when they are wettest. And, as a bonus, a web spun in the moist morning air is better able to soak up water for the following day.

The water taken up by the spider silk also helps to capture prey. The glue with which spiders coat their webs is stickier when wet. Maximising the water content of the thread thus increases the chances of catching and keeping unwary flies. It also contributes to the extraordinary elasticity which allows a web to intercept flying insects without snapping.

Spiders' webs are made from two different types of silk: structural and capture thread. Structural silk is rigid and gives the web strength. It is the capture silk that does the clever tricks. It can stretch without strain by up to four times its original length to absorb the momentum of an incoming fly. It then springs back without sagging when the strain is removed.

The presence of water is crucial to these properties. The researchers had previously found that a liquid droplet on the stretched silk acts as a miniature windlass, reeling it back in by the power of its surface tension. They also knew that water was necessary for the capture web to be able to stretch in the first place. But they did not know why.

So they enlisted the help of some chemists from Cambridge, who discovered that the capture web has regions of highly mobile molecules, more like a liquid than a solid. The chemists believe that these molecules are flexible "springs" connecting rigid crystalline regions of the silk. With a little more research, they should be able to work out the composition of both the flexible and the rigid units. Armed with this information, they might even be able to produce their own drinkable stretch material one day.
questions.prompt: Spiders' webs ____.
choices: are eaten when it rains heavily
are eaten for their water content
absorb less moisture early in the day
questions.explanation: The researchers concluded that spiders "are not eating their webs; they are drinking them".
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.
questions.source: UN Language Proficiency Examination (English) practice paper

Webs are consumed in the humid pre-dawn because this is when they are wettest. And, as a bonus, a web spun in the moist morning air is better able to soak up water for the following day.

The water taken up by the spider silk also helps to capture prey. The glue with which spiders coat their webs is stickier when wet. Maximising the water content of the thread thus increases the chances of catching and keeping unwary flies. It also contributes to the extraordinary elasticity which allows a web to intercept flying insects without snapping.

Spiders' webs are made from two different types of silk: structural and capture thread. Structural silk is rigid and gives the web strength. It is the capture silk that does the clever tricks. It can stretch without strain by up to four times its original length to absorb the momentum of an incoming fly. It then springs back without sagging when the strain is removed.

The presence of water is crucial to these properties. The researchers had previously found that a liquid droplet on the stretched silk acts as a miniature windlass, reeling it back in by the power of its surface tension. They also knew that water was necessary for the capture web to be able to stretch in the first place. But they did not know why.

So they enlisted the help of some chemists from Cambridge, who discovered that the capture web has regions of highly mobile molecules, more like a liquid than a solid. The chemists believe that these molecules are flexible "springs" connecting rigid crystalline regions of the silk. With a little more research, they should be able to work out the composition of both the flexible and the rigid units. Armed with this information, they might even be able to produce their own drinkable stretch material one day.
questions.prompt: The word "it" in the phrase "reeling it back in" (paragraph 7) means ____.
questions.explanation: The droplet acts as a windlass "reeling it back in": what is reeled in is the stretched silk.
questions.tip: Pick the option that is directly supported by the text. Options that are partly true, too extreme ("all", "never") or not mentioned are traps.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that best completes or corrects the sentence.

questions.passage:
There is a place forty kilometres north-east of Portland, Victoria, which makes for an unusual visit. It is Lake Condah. Here are to be found remains of aboriginal settlements: the circular stone bases of several hundred huts, rock-lined water channels, and stone tools chipped from rock not normally found in the area. One of the attractions of Lake Condah long ago was its fish and the most startling evidence of aboriginal technology and engineering to be found there are the systems built to trap fish.

Water courses had been constructed by redirecting streams, building stone sides and even scraping out new channels. At strategic spots, they piled rocks across the water courses to create weirs and build funnels to channel eels and fish into conical baskets. This is an eel-fishing technique which has hardly changed to the present day. Beside some of the larger traps, there are the outlines of rectangular, stone-lined ponds, probably to hold fish and keep them fresh.

On the bluffs overlooking the lake, stone circles are all that remain of ancient dwellings. Not all of the stones were quarried locally. The huts vary in size, but all have gaps for doorways located on the lee side, away from the prevailing wind. One theory is that the stone walls were only waist to shoulder high, with the top roofed by branches and possibly packed with mud.

The site presents a picture of a semi-settled people quite different from the stereotype of nomadic hunter-gatherers of the desert.

questions.explanation: A stereotype is a fixed, commonly held (standard) view of a group, here of desert hunter-gatherers.

questions.passage:
Between us there was, as I have already said somewhere, the bond of the sea. Besides holding our hearts together through long periods of separation, it had the effect of making us tolerant of each other's yarns, and even convictions. The Lawyer, the best of old fellows, had, because of his many years and many virtues, the only cushion on deck, and was lying on the only rug. The Accountant had brought out already a box of dominoes, and was toying architecturally with the bones. Marlow sat cross-legged right aft, leaning against the mizzen-mast. He had sunken cheeks, a yellow complexion, a straight back, an ascetic aspect, and, with his arms dropped, the palms of hands outwards, resembled an idol. The Director, satisfied the anchor had good hold, made his way aft and sat down amongst us. We exchanged a few words lazily.

Afterwards there was silence on board the yacht. For some reason or other we did not begin that game of dominoes. We felt meditative, and fit for nothing but placid staring. The day was ending in a serenity of still and exquisite brilliance. The water shone pacifically; the sky, without a speck, was a benign immensity of unstained light; the very mist on the Essex marshes was like a gauzy and radiant fabric, hung from the wooded rises inland, and draping the low shores in diaphanous folds. Only the gloom to the west, brooding over the upper reaches, became more sombre every minute, as if angered by the approach of the sun.

(From "Heart of Darkness" by Joseph Conrad)

questions.passage:
Among predatory dinosaurs, few flesh-eaters were bigger, faster and nastier than the "tyrant lizard" of popular imagination, the Tyrannosaurus Rex. At least, that is what we have been led to believe.

Now research suggests that, far from being the Ferrari of dinosaurs, Tyrannosaurus Rex, whose ferocious reputation has fascinated generations of schoolchildren, was in fact a cumbersome creature with a usual running speed of twenty-five kilometres an hour. This is a mere snail's pace compared with modern animals such as the cheetah.

Unlike some of the predators of today's African savannah, which can change direction almost immediately, the dinosaur would have had to turn slowly or risk tumbling over. And while a human can spin forty-five degrees in a twentieth of a second, a Tyrannosaurus would have taken as much as two seconds, as it would have been hampered by its long tail. Thankfully, however, all its prey, such as triceratops, would have been afflicted with the same lack of speed and agility.

The findings were reached after researchers used computer modelling and biomechanical calculations to work out the dinosaur's speed, agility and weight. They based their calculations on measurements taken from a fossil dinosaur representative of an average Tyrannosaurus and concluded the creatures probably weighed between six and eight tonnes.

Calculations of the leg muscles suggest that the animal would have had a top speed of forty kilometres an hour, which is nothing compared to a cheetah's one hundred kilometres an hour.

questions.explanation: A Ferrari is a fast sports car, so the nickname implies speed and agility, which the research contradicts.

questions.passage:
"Anne," cried Mary, still at her window, "there is Mrs Clay, I am sure, standing under the colonnade, and a gentleman with her. I saw them turn the corner from Bath Street just now. They seemed deep in talk. Who is it? Come, and tell me. Good heavens! I recollect. It is Mr Elliot himself."

"No," cried Anne, quickly, "it cannot be Mr Elliot, I assure you. He was to leave Bath at nine this morning, and does not come back till to-morrow."

As she spoke, she felt that Captain Wentworth was looking at her, the consciousness of which vexed and embarrassed her, and made her regret that she had said so much, simple as it was.

Mary, resenting that she should be supposed not to know her own cousin, began talking very warmly about the family features, and protesting still more positively that it was Mr Elliot, calling again upon Anne to come and look for herself, but Anne did not mean to stir, and tried to be cool and unconcerned. Her distress returned, however, on perceiving smiles and intelligent glances pass between two or three of the lady visitors, as if they believed themselves quite in the secret. It was evident that the report concerning her had spread, and a short pause succeeded, which seemed to ensure that it would now spread farther.

"Do come, Anne," cried Mary, "come and look yourself. You will be too late if you do not make haste. They are parting; they are shaking hands. He is turning away. Not know Mr Elliot, indeed! You seem to have forgotten all about Lyme."

To pacify Mary, and perhaps screen her own embarrassment, Anne did move quietly to the window. She was just in time to ascertain that it really was Mr Elliot, which she had never believed, before he disappeared on one side, as Mrs Clay walked quickly off on the other; and checking the surprise which she could not but feel at such an appearance of friendly conference between two persons of totally opposite interest, she calmly said, "Yes, it is Mr Elliot, certainly. He has changed his hour of going, I suppose, that is all, or I may be mistaken, I might not attend;" and walked back to her chair, recomposed, and with the comfortable hope of having acquitted herself well.

(From "Persuasion" by Jane Austen)

it was highly unlikely that Mr Elliot would be a friend of Mrs Clay.
questions.explanation: Anne's stated reason is: "He was to leave Bath at nine this morning". Mary knows her own cousin, so (a) is wrong.

Mary, resenting that she should be supposed not to know her own cousin, began talking very warmly about the family features, and protesting still more positively that it was Mr Elliot, calling again upon Anne to come and look for herself, but Anne did not mean to stir, and tried to be cool and unconcerned. Her distress returned, however, on perceiving smiles and intelligent glances pass between two or three of the lady visitors, as if they believed themselves quite in the secret. It was evident that the report concerning her had spread, and a short pause succeeded, which seemed to ensure that it would now spread farther.

"Do come, Anne," cried Mary, "come and look yourself. You will be too late if you do not make haste. They are parting; they are shaking hands. He is turning away. Not know Mr Elliot, indeed! You seem to have forgotten all about Lyme."

To pacify Mary, and perhaps screen her own embarrassment, Anne did move quietly to the window. She was just in time to ascertain that it really was Mr Elliot, which she had never believed, before he disappeared on one side, as Mrs Clay walked quickly off on the other; and checking the surprise which she could not but feel at such an appearance of friendly conference between two persons of totally opposite interest, she calmly said, "Yes, it is Mr Elliot, certainly. questions.passage: A hare was very popular with the other beasts who all claimed to be her friend, but one day she heard the hounds approaching and hoped to escape them with the help of her many friends. "What are friends for," she asked herself, "if not to help out in time of need?" Furthermore, most of her friends were big and brave, so at least one should be able to help. First she went to the horse, and asked him to carry her away from the hounds on his back. But he declined, stating that he had important work to do for his master. "I feel sure," he said, "that all your other friends will come to your assistance." She then applied to the bull, and hoped that he would repel the hounds with his horns. The bull replied: "I am very sorry, but I have an appointment with a lady. However, I feel sure that our friend the goat will do what you want." The goat, however, feared that his back might be harmed if he took her upon it. The ram, he felt sure, was the proper friend to apply to. So she went to the ram and told him the case. The ram replied: "Another time, my dear friend. I do not like to interfere on the present occasion, as hounds have been known to eat sheep as well as hares." The hare then applied, as a last hope, to the calf, who regretted that he was unable to help her. He did not like to take the responsibility upon himself, as so many older persons had declined the task. By this time the hounds were quite near, so the hare had to take to her heels. Luckily, she escaped.

questions.passage:
When I returned to the common the sun was setting. The crowd about the pit had increased, and stood out black against the lemon yellow of the sky, a couple of hundred people, perhaps. There were raised voices, and some sort of struggle appeared to be going on about the pit. As I drew nearer I heard Stent's voice: "Keep back! Keep back!" A boy came running towards me. "It's movin'," he said to me as he passed; "it's screwin' and screwin' out. I don't like it. I'm goin' home, I am." I went on to the crowd. There were really, I should think, two or three hundred people elbowing and jostling one another, the one or two ladies there being by no means the least active. "He's fallen in the pit!" cried some one. "Keep back!" said several. The crowd swayed a little, and I elbowed my way through. Everyone seemed greatly excited.

The end of the cylinder was being screwed out from within. Nearly two feet of shining screw projected. Somebody blundered against me, and I narrowly missed being pitched onto the top of the screw. I turned, and as I did so the screw must have come out, for the lid of the cylinder fell upon the gravel with a ringing concussion. For a moment that circular cavity seemed perfectly black. I had the sunset in my eyes.

I think everyone expected to see a man emerge, possibly something a little unlike us terrestrial men, but in all essentials a man. I know I did. But, looking, I presently saw something stirring within the shadow: greyish billowy movements, one above another, and then two luminous disks like eyes. Then something resembling a little grey snake, about the thickness of a walking stick, coiled up out of the writhing middle, and wriggled in the air towards me, and then another.

A sudden chill came over me. There was a loud shriek from a woman behind. I half turned, keeping my eyes fixed upon the cylinder still, from which other tentacles were now projecting, and began pushing my way back from the edge of the pit. I saw astonishment giving place to horror on the faces of the people about me. There was a general movement backwards.

A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder. Two large dark-coloured eyes were regarding me steadfastly. The peculiar V-shaped mouth with its pointed upper lip, the absence of brow ridges, the absence of a chin beneath the wedgelike lower lip, the incessant quivering of this mouth, the Gorgon groups of tentacles, the tumultuous breathing of the lungs in a strange atmosphere, the evident heaviness and painfulness of movement due to the greater gravitational energy of the earth, above all, the extraordinary intensity of the immense eyes, were at once vital, intense, inhuman, crippled and monstrous. There was something fungoid in the oily brown skin, something in the clumsy deliberation of the tedious movements unspeakably nasty. Even at this first encounter, this first glimpse, I was overcome with disgust and dread.

(From "The War of the Worlds" by H. G. Wells)
questions.prompt: This is part of a science fiction story. The most important clue to this would be
choices: something unscrewing the cylinder from within.
the sense of terror and apprehension in the crowd.
the author's feelings of disgust and dread.
questions.explanation: A living creature from another planet ("the greater gravitational energy of the earth") is the clearest science-fiction element.

questions.passage:
The debate on whether Australia will have a nation-wide carbon trading scheme ended last week with the government committed to a national emissions scheme from 2012. However, the decision-making as to how we power the economy in a carbon constrained world is only just beginning. Fossil fuels like coal and oil have underpinned our economic growth and standard of living for decades. The current resources boom is there because other countries want our fossil fuels, and for all these reasons it is profitable to keep mining them. Ironically, the income may help develop the technologies to replace them, but it is a matter of which and when.

Almost certainly, in the race to reduce emissions, new technologies such as solar, wind and geothermal (heat from rocks) power will compete against gas, clean coal and perhaps nuclear energy to win the hearts and minds of the business world. In the end, business will favour whatever is a cheap, abundant and reliable solution. You can imagine the lobbying that will ensue from the different interest groups, to attract business capital and government support so that their technology wins out. There may be many collapsed ventures and lost fortunes along the way.

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels "have underpinned our economic growth and standard of living". The passage names alternatives, so (a) is wrong, and it does not say fuels are cheap.

questions.passage:
One of the modern world's intriguing sources of mystery has been aeroplanes vanishing in mid-flight. One of the more famous of these was the disappearance in 1937 of a pioneer woman aviator, Amelia Earhart. On the second last stage of an attempted round the world flight, she had radioed her position as she and her navigator searched desperately for their destination, a tiny island in the Pacific.

The plane never arrived at Howland Island. Did it crash and sink after running out of fuel? Did Earhart have enough fuel to set down on some other island on her radioed course? Or did she end up somewhere else altogether? One fanciful theory had her being captured by the Japanese in the Marshall Islands and later executed as an American spy; another had her living out her days under an assumed name as a housewife in New Jersey.

Seventy years after Earhart's disappearance, "myth busters" continue to search for her. She was the best-known American woman pilot in the world. Her disappearance has been the subject of at least fifty books, countless magazine and newspaper articles, and TV documentaries. It is seen by journalists as the last great American mystery.

There were reports of distress calls from the Phoenix Islands made on Earhart's radio frequency for days after she vanished. Some say the plane could have broadcast only if it were on land, not in the water. No-one was able to trace the calls at the time, so whether Earhart was on land in the Phoenix Islands or there was a hoaxer using her radio remains a mystery. Others dismiss the radio calls as bogus and insist Earhart and her navigator ditched in the water near Howland Island. At that depth, the fuselage would still be in shiny, pristine condition if ever anyone were able to locate it.

Whatever the explanation, the prospect of finding the remains is unsettling to many. To recover skeletal remains or personal effects would be a grisly experience and an intrusion. As one investigator has put it, "I'm convinced that the mystery is part of what keeps us interested."

Until widespread clearing of land began after 1861, the Tweed Valley, from the beach dunes to the mountains, was covered by dense wetland forests and rainforest. The rainforest had plenty of red cedar, which grew along the river banks and over the floodplains and foothills. Some of these trees were huge, up to sixty metres tall and as much as two thousand years old. Cedar was highly valued for its light weight, rich pink to red colours and interesting grain patterns. The tall trees provided magnificent lengths for the mills. Much early Australian furniture was made from cedar.

The timber of the Tweed Valley was felled close to the river banks and then was tied and floated downstream to the river mouth for shipping to the big cities. The river provided the only means of removing the timber, because the felled trees were so bulky.

By the 1870s, the cedar industry was in decline. Land cleared for farming was on the increase and easily obtainable, and large cedar trees were becoming scarce. It was purely an extractive industry, which put nothing back.

questions.passage:
When someone asks us where we are from or what we do, most of us mention the town or city where we live, our occupation, where we attended school, or our family heritage. We respond in terms of human communities, cultures, and geopolitical boundaries. We seldom, if ever, describe ourselves in terms of our ecological status in the natural world. We humans have so completely ordered, designed, and defined our physical environs and social milieu that our ecological connections have slipped from consciousness. Perhaps this is why we seem so unaware of our impact on nature and our rapid destruction of natural systems. We simply do not perceive ourselves as being part of the natural order of beings.

All of us live within ecological systems, or "ecosystems," and through our commerce, food distribution, and use of natural resources we each indirectly participate in the custodianship of many ecosystems worldwide. Ironically, we are simultaneously the most potent forces within most ecosystems, and yet nearly oblivious to the ecological effects of our daily lifestyles. There has never been a time when a deep understanding of ecosystems and our roles within them has been more critical. Indeed, the world's freshwater ecosystems are so degraded that their ability to support plant and animal life, including humans, is viewed by many as being in peril. Learning about ecosystems is more than an expected focus in biology classes; it has become a study in survival.

(Excerpted from a 2002 article about ecosystems)

Claude backed the little Ford car out of its shed, ran it up to the horse-tank, and began to throw water on the mud-crusted wheels and windshield. While he was at work the two hired men, Dan and Jerry, came shambling down the hill to feed the stock. Jerry was grumbling and swearing about something, but Claude wrung out his wet rags and, beyond a nod, paid no attention to them. Somehow his father always managed to have the roughest and dirtiest hired men in the country working for him. Claude had a grievance against Jerry just now, because of his treatment of one of the horses.

Molly was a faithful old mare, the mother of many colts; Claude and his younger brother had learned to ride on her. This man Jerry, taking her out to work one morning, let her step on a board with a nail sticking up in it. He pulled the nail out of her foot, said nothing to anybody, and drove her to the cultivator all day. Now she had been standing in her stall for weeks, patiently suffering, her body wretchedly thin, and her leg swollen until it looked like an elephant's. Jerry had not been discharged, and he exhibited the poor animal as if she were a credit to him.

When Claude reached the kitchen, a moment later Mr. Wheeler came down the enclosed stairway and walked the length of the table to his own place. He was a very large man, taller and broader than any of his neighbours. His florid face was clean shaven, likely to be a trifle tobacco-stained about the mouth, and it was conspicuous both for good-nature and coarse humour, and for an imperturbable physical composure. Nobody in the county had ever seen Nat Wheeler flustered about anything, and nobody had ever heard him speak with complete seriousness.

(From "One of Ours" by Willa Cather, 1922)

questions.explanation: "Hardly" makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive: "does she".
questions.tip: Repeat the auxiliary of the statement (or use do/does/did), reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Watch for negative words like "never", "hardly" and "nobody".

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag.
questions.prompt: Let's go to the library, ___?
questions.explanation: Suggestions with "Let's" take the tag "shall we".
questions.tip: Repeat the auxiliary of the statement (or use do/does/did), reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Watch for negative words like "never", "hardly" and "nobody".

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag.
questions.prompt: Nobody called while I was out, ___?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" is negative, so the tag is positive, and it is referred to with "they".
questions.tip: Repeat the auxiliary of the statement (or use do/does/did), reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Watch for negative words like "never", "hardly" and "nobody".

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag.
questions.prompt: I am your friend, ___?
questions.explanation: The standard tag after "I am" is "aren't I".
questions.tip: Repeat the auxiliary of the statement (or use do/does/did), reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Watch for negative words like "never", "hardly" and "nobody".

questions.instruction: Choose the correct question tag.
questions.prompt: Everyone has submitted, ___?
questions.explanation: "Everyone" takes "they" in the tag, so the auxiliary becomes "have": "haven't they".
questions.tip: Repeat the auxiliary of the statement (or use do/does/did), reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Watch for negative words like "never", "hardly" and "nobody".

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is correctly capitalised and punctuated.
questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: We visited the University of Lagos in December.
We visited the university of Lagos in december.
We visited the University Of Lagos In December.
we visited the University of Lagos in December.
questions.explanation: The full name of the university is a proper noun, and months take a capital; "of" stays lower case in a title.
questions.tip: Capitalise names of particular people, places, days, months, languages and titles used with a name. Do not capitalise seasons or general words like "university" used on their own.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is correctly capitalised and punctuated.
questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: My uncle, who lives in Abuja is a doctor.
My uncle who lives in Abuja, is a doctor.
My uncle, who lives in Abuja, is a doctor.
My Uncle, who lives in Abuja, is a doctor.
questions.explanation: A non-defining clause is enclosed by a pair of commas, and "uncle" is not a title before a name here.
questions.tip: Capitalise names of particular people, places, days, months, languages and titles used with a name. Do not capitalise seasons or general words like "university" used on their own.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is correctly capitalised and punctuated.
questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: The students' hostel is near the Faculty of Arts.
The students's hostel is near the Faculty of Arts.
The students hostel is near the Faculty of Arts.
The student's' hostel is near the faculty of arts.
questions.explanation: For a plural noun ending in s, the possessive apostrophe follows the s: "students'". The faculty's full name is capitalised.
questions.tip: Capitalise names of particular people, places, days, months, languages and titles used with a name. Do not capitalise seasons or general words like "university" used on their own.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is correctly capitalised and punctuated.
questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: Its' clear that the dog has hurt its leg.
It's clear that the dog has hurt it's leg.
It's clear that the dog has hurt its leg.
Its clear that the dog has hurt it's leg.
questions.explanation: "It's" means "it is"; the possessive "its" has no apostrophe.
questions.tip: Capitalise names of particular people, places, days, months, languages and titles used with a name. Do not capitalise seasons or general words like "university" used on their own.

questions.instruction: Choose the option that is correctly capitalised and punctuated.
questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: we study English, French and Yoruba in the harmattan.
We study english, french and yoruba in the harmattan.
We study English, French and Yoruba in the harmattan.
We study English, French and Yoruba in the Harmattan Season.
questions.explanation: Names of languages are capitalised; seasons, including the harmattan, normally are not.
questions.tip: Capitalise names of particular people, places, days, months, languages and titles used with a name. Do not capitalise seasons or general words like "university" used on their own.
